ch06.card: Part 5 of 10. Deciding when it is done.
ch06.s01.c1: Picture a student in an exam. Hand it in too early and you are wrong. So who decides when to stop? Our model thinks in rounds, one lap at a time.
ch06.s01.c2: The stop switch decides when to stop. Think of it as a bell.
ch06.s01.c3: It is built, but it has never been run, so it is not tested.
ch06.s02.c1: The older design had a dial: the same number of rounds for every question, set by hand. That was 12 in the tested model, and 8 in another.
ch06.s02.c2: Easy questions may need fewer rounds. Hard questions may need more. This is a picture only.
ch06.s03.c1: What if we turn the dial down? We tried it on one trained copy, with no new practice.
ch06.s03.c2: Scores are points out of 100, on 6,040 questions kept aside. We call that set pooled-5.
ch06.s03.c3: Trained at 12 rounds, it scored 73.01. With 2 rounds, 29.30. With 1 round, 20.00. With 0 rounds, 0.66.
ch06.s04.c1: Now harder questions. Chain-5 is a set of 1,000 multi-step questions, scored on the same trained copy.
ch06.s04.c2: On pooled-5, 1 round scored 20.00. On chain-5 it scored 0.0, and 1.1 at 2 rounds.
ch06.s04.c3: At the full 12 rounds, chain-5 scored 99.9. So this copy needed more rounds on multi-step questions than on pooled-5.
ch06.s05.c1: More thinking never hurts? Not so. Older models were trained for 8 rounds, and on two copies the score on practice-like questions stopped rising at 8 rounds.
ch06.s05.c2: On all 8 copies we checked, those two and six more, 16 rounds scored 0.8 to 1.9 points lower than 8.
ch06.s05.c3: So too few rounds hurt, and too many may hurt too.
ch06.s06.c1: How does the bell work? After every round, the stop switch, a small head, reads one of the thinker's note cards.
ch06.s06.c2: It gives a number from 0 to 1. At 0.5 or more, the bell rings.
ch06.s06.c3: It always runs at least 1 round, and never more than 32.
ch06.s06.c4: The stop switch has 257 numbers when each card has 256, and 513 when each has 512.
ch06.s07.c1: Built version: one bell for the whole answer. New design: one bell per turn.
ch06.s07.c2: Built, not tested: the thinker may call an outside calculator, from round 2 up to 32.
ch06.s07.c3: Built: about a quarter add 0 to 2 rounds before a call. New design: the talker writes calls.
ch06.s08.c1: How does it learn when to ring? Every round gets a label, like a teacher's note: stop, or keep going.
ch06.s08.c2: The label says stop when the answer is right now, or when no later round is right.
ch06.s08.c3: So the stop switch is also taught to stop on questions it cannot solve.
ch06.s09.c1: Here is a trap. Practice uses batches, and some batches run only 8 rounds. There, a question first right at round 10 looks never right.
ch06.s09.c2: So the label says stop at round 1, which is wrong, and the stop switch would learn to stop too early.
ch06.s09.c3: Fix: the stop switch learns only from batches that run all 32 rounds, about 1 in 4.
ch06.s10.c1: Will the bell ring too soon? The label only sees the rounds a question actually ran.
ch06.s10.c2: So a stop that fires early may never be shown a later right answer. That is only suggested.
ch06.s10.c3: The first run is planned to report how often questions stop early, and their answers. This is reported only, not a pass mark.
ch06.s11.c1: Before any run, we wrote down what counts as success. These key pass marks are targets, not results.
ch06.s11.c2: On average, 1-step questions must use at most half the rounds of the longest ones. The code says 11 steps, and the plan says 12.
ch06.s11.c3: Always-32 is the same model forced to think all 32 rounds. Practised questions must be within 1 point. Longer chains, within 2.
ch06.s11.c4: It fails if it never stops early, meaning rounds within 10% of 32, or if longer chains fall over 5 below always-32.
ch06.s12.c1: If it fails? No build switch removes the stop.
ch06.s12.c2: A trained copy can still be run with the stop ignored and a forced number of rounds, as a test.
ch06.s12.c3: The nearest model with no stop is the outside-calculator model, T1SDR, with a fixed 8 rounds.
ch06.s12.c4: The stop has never run. Its first run is planned after the separate G1 size test finishes.
ch06.s13.c1: Could one thinker be quick and careful? People talk about fast thinking and slow thinking. Few rounds is like the fast kind, many rounds like the slow kind.
ch06.s13.c2: We suggest one looped thinker gives both, so no separate fast and slow model is needed. That is suggested, not tested.
ch06.s13.c3: To remember: the stop switch decides, the limit is 32 rounds, and the stop is built but not yet run. Next: the talker, only a stand-in today.
